# Ezekiel 2 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Verse 1

**“Son of man,” He said to me, “stand up on your feet and I will speak to you.”**

- **“Son of man”** — This title appears 93 times in Ezekiel and elsewhere only once in Daniel (Dan 8:17). It is a Hebraism emphasising the prophet's mere humanity, frailty, and insignificance before the majesty of God. "Son of" indicates "partaking of the nature of," so combined with *adam* it means simply "human being" or "mortal." It stands in deliberate contrast to the overwhelming glory Ezekiel has just witnessed in chapter 1. By New Testament times the phrase had taken on messianic overtones (from Daniel 7:13), and Jesus used it of Himself some 80 times — yet Ezekiel's usage is the simpler, humbler sense. JFB adds that the title was likely drawn from Chaldean usage during the Babylonian exile and that God used it "lest he should be exalted through the abundance of the revelations" (cf. 2 Cor 12:7). Gill notes Ezekiel is an eminent type of Christ and that none but Ezekiel (and once Daniel) is called by this name among the prophets.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_21-10

- **“Stand up on your feet”** — Ezekiel had fallen prostrate at the vision of God's glory (Ezek 1:28). God now commands him to rise. The shift is from awestruck prostration (servility) to attentive readiness (service). As G. Campbell Morgan put it: "That prostrate soul was called to a new attitude… that of standing erect before God in order that face to face he might receive the word of God." Trapp adds: "Oracles are for standers, not prostrate ones. They require utmost attention of body, intention of mind, and retention of memory." Humiliation before God is followed by exaltation to service (cf. Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5).
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_21-10

---

## Verse 2

**And as He spoke to me, the Spirit entered me and set me on my feet, and I heard Him speaking to me.**

- **The Spirit entered me** — God first commanded Ezekiel to stand, then provided the enablement through the Holy Spirit. The sequence is significant: God's commands carry with them His enabling power. JFB observes: "The divine word is ever accompanied by the Spirit (Gen 1:2-3)." Gill stresses that although the divine word commanded him to stand, it was actually the Spirit who set him on his feet, underscoring that "the word, though it is the word of God… is ineffectual without the Spirit."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_21-10

- **The Spirit "entered" rather than merely "came upon"** — Guzik (EnduringWord) notes this same pattern of Spirit and Word working together marks believers today. Precept Austin observes that in the Old Testament the Spirit did not indwell all believers permanently but came upon selected persons for divine service (contrast David's prayer in Ps 51:11 with the New Covenant sealing of Eph 1:13-14). The Expositor's Bible Commentary notes the LXX has "the Spirit came upon me" rather than "entered," though the idea is the same.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_21-10
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-2.html

- **"I heard Him speaking"** — The Spirit's empowerment enabled Ezekiel not only to stand physically but to hear with spiritual understanding. As Gill notes: "the Spirit, who searches the deep things of God, reveals them to his ministers, and causes them to understand the word of Christ."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm

---

## Verse 3

**“Son of man,” He said to me, “I am sending you to the Israelites, to a rebellious nation that has rebelled against Me. To this very day they and their fathers have rebelled against Me.”**

- **"I am sending you"** — The Hebrew verb *salah* (send) was the technical term for commissioning a prophetic messenger. As Block notes (cited in Guzik): "Prophets functioned primarily as messengers of God, and the critical issue in the conflict between true and false prophets was which persons had actually been commissioned by Yahweh."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/

- **"A rebellious nation"** — The Hebrew reads literally "rebellious nations" (plural *goyim*). The word *goyim* is normally used of heathen Gentiles, and applying it to Israel is a sharp pejorative: apart from faith in and fidelity to Yahweh, Israel had become indistinguishable from pagan nations. JFB compares Isa 1:10 where Israel is called "Sodom and Gomorrah," and Hosea 1:9 where they become "Lo-ammi" — not My people. Calvin adds that *goyim* was to the Jews a term of utter reproach, meaning "profane," "rejected," and "pollution" — so this would have stung deeply. Precept Austin notes the Hebrew *marad* (rebel) conveys open, formidable resistance to authority.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_21-10

- **"They and their fathers have transgressed against Me to this very day"** — The word "transgressed" (*pasha*) is the strongest Hebrew term for covenant violation, used in diplomatic contexts for treaty-breaking. Both generations stand guilty; the present generation cannot blame their fathers alone. Gill calls this an "aggravation of their rebellion."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_21-10

---

## Verse 4

**"They are obstinate and stubborn children. I am sending you to them, and you are to say to them, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says.’"**

- **"Obstinate and stubborn"** — Literally "hard of face and firm of heart" (or "stiff-hearted"). "Hard of face" describes the shameless, brazen person who refuses to lower his gaze even when guilty. "Firm of heart" describes the stubborn, unyielding will that refuses to give way. Gill comments that they had "a whore's forehead, and refused to be ashamed" (cf. Jer 3:3) and their hearts were "like an adamant stone, and harder than the nether millstone; impenitent, obdurate, and inflexible." JFB observes God opposes His own command and name ("Thus saith the Lord GOD") to the people's obstinacy: "Duties are ours; events are God's."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-2.html

- **"This is what the Lord GOD says"** — The prophetic messenger formula. Ezekiel is to speak not his own thoughts but God's precise words. The title "Lord GOD" (Adonai Yahweh) asserts divine authority against the people's rebellion.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm

---

## Verse 5

**"And whether they listen or refuse to listen—for they are a rebellious house—they will know that a prophet has been among them."**

- **"Whether they hear or whether they refuse"** — Ezekiel is freed from the burden of results. His responsibility is faithfulness in delivery, not success in persuasion. Guzik notes: "Being the messenger, he was not ultimately responsible for how the message was received — only to demonstrate that a prophet has been among them."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/

- **"They will know that a prophet has been among them"** — The primary vindication would come through fulfilled predictions (especially the destruction of Jerusalem). Block (cited by Guzik): "This vindication will obviously not come through masses of repentant converts… All that remains is the traditional sign of a true prophet — the fulfillment of his predictions." Clarke adds a twofold purpose: they would know (1) that God in mercy had given due warning, and (2) that they themselves were inexcusable for not heeding it. The Expositor's Bible Commentary expands: though it seems a poor reward for years of contention, "it was also to be the beginning of better days," for once recognised as a true prophet, his later words of restoration would also be heeded.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-2.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm

---

## Verse 6

**"But you, son of man, do not be afraid of them or their words. Do not be afraid, though briers and thorns surround you, and you dwell among scorpions. Do not be afraid of their words or dismayed by their presence, though they are a rebellious house."**

- **"Do not be afraid" repeated** — Poole notes the admonition against sinful fear is given four times in this verse, "lest Ezekiel should forget, or we in like case should fail of our duty." Guzik observes that Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel all received "depressing calls" — they were needed in desperate situations and had to be prepared for rejection and threats.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/

- **"Briers and thorns… scorpions"** — These are metaphors for the people's words and treatment of the prophet. Gill explains: wicked men are like briers and thorns — "grieving, pricking, and distressing to good men… useless and unprofitable, and fit fuel for everlasting burning." Scorpions are "subtle, venomous, and mischievous, which have stings in their tails… continually thrusting out and striking with, that they may lose no opportunity of doing hurt." JFB notes "briers" comes from a root meaning "to sting" as nettles do, and scorpions are a reptile about six inches long with a deadly sting at the end of the tail.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm

- **"Dismayed by their presence"** — The Hebrew verb is strong, meaning "to be shattered" or broken. God warns against being psychologically broken by the hostile looks and presence of the rebellious people.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/

---

## Verse 7

**"But speak My words to them, whether they listen or refuse to listen, for they are rebellious."**

- **"Speak My words"** — The emphasis is not on Ezekiel's eloquence, opinions, or innovations but on faithfully delivering God's words. Gill comments: "Not his own words, but those the Lord should put into his mouth."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm

- **"Most rebellious"** — Literally "rebellion itself" (the abstract noun used for emphasis). JFB says it is "its very essence." Gill compares Rom 8:7 where the carnal mind is called "enmity itself against God."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm

- Guzik draws the parallel with Paul's charge to Timothy: "preach the word… in season and out of season" (2 Tim 4:2). Acceptance or rejection must not determine the prophet's work.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/

---

## Verse 8

**"And you, son of man, listen to what I tell you. Do not be rebellious like that rebellious house. Open your mouth and eat what I give you."**

- **"Do not be rebellious like that rebellious house"** — Ezekiel faces the same temptation as the people: to resist God's word. If they rebel by refusing to hear, he might rebel by refusing to speak. Guzik: "He had to be surrendered to the LORD even if they were not, indeed especially if they were not."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/

- **"Open your mouth and eat what I give you"** — The command to eat the scroll is a dramatic symbolic act. Unlike Jeremiah who had God's words put into his mouth (Jer 1:9), Ezekiel is given a written scroll to digest. JFB explains: "The idea is to possess himself fully of the message and digest it in the mind; not literal eating, but such an appropriation of its unsavory contents that they should become, as it were, part of himself, so as to impart them the more vividly to his hearers." Guzik elaborates that eating the scroll pictures deliberate action, readiness to receive, internal reception, repetitious chewing, complete reception, digestion, necessity, sweetness, and strength/nourishment. Gill's practical note: "Christ gives his ministers and people nothing but what is wholesome; his doctrines are wholesome words and may be eaten without fear."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm

- The Expositor's Bible Commentary clarifies that the eating of the book signifies not a mechanical dictation but "the self-surrender of the prophet to his vocation as a vehicle of the word of Jehovah." The message must become his own — "God's ultimately, but Ezekiel must make it his own, work it into the very fibre of his being."
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-2.html

## Verse 9

**"Then I looked and saw a hand reaching out to me, and in it was a scroll,"**

- **"A hand"** — In the vision of Ezekiel 1, the only hands mentioned belonged to the cherubim surrounding God's throne. Guzik notes it is unclear whether this is the hand of God or an angelic hand. Gill identifies it as the hand of Christ Himself in a visionary way. Vawter and Hoppe (cited by Guzik) say: "Whether it is actually the hand of the Lord or simply a figure made necessary by the visionary symbolism is not important. The scroll, of course, represents the word which Ezekiel is to proclaim."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm

- **"A scroll"** — The ancient book form: parchment or papyrus rolled around a stick. Gill notes this was a symbol of the prophecy Ezekiel was to deliver — it came from heaven, and the hand that delivered it would also protect him. Block (cited by Guzik) says the scroll was "probably made from papyrus rather than skin, since the former was the more common scroll material in biblical times."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/

---

## Verse 10

**"which He unrolled before me. And written on the front and back of it were words of lamentation, mourning, and woe."**

- **"Written on the front and back"** — Normally scrolls were written on one side only (the inside when rolled). Writing on both sides indicated the fullness and completeness of the message. Feinberg (cited by Guzik): "the message of the Lord was so full of threatenings and woes that both sides had to be utilized." Block adds: "Ezekiel may not modify it with his own comments, nor does God allow himself any room for adjustments." JFB similarly: "so full was God's message of impending woes that it was written also on the back." This detail recalls the scroll in Revelation 5:1, also written on both sides.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm

- **"Lamentation, mourning, and woe"** — These three terms summarise the content of Ezekiel's early ministry (chapters 1–24), which focuses on judgment against Jerusalem before its fall in 586 BC. Peake's Commentary notes that this "faithfully describe(s) the general contents and temper of Ezekiel's message throughout the earlier part of his ministry." The Talmud (cited by Gill) interpreted "lamentations" as the punishments of the righteous in this world, "mourning" as the gift of reward to the righteous in the world to come, and "woe" as the punishments of the wicked in the world to come. Clarke (cited by Guzik) contrasts this with the New Covenant gospel: "What a mercy to have that which is emphatically called, the glad tidings, the good news! Christ Jesus is come into the world to save sinners… Here are rejoicings, thanksgivings, and exultation."
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-2/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-2.html

## Points Where Traditions Differ

I was unable to retrieve full tradition-specific content from many of the denominational sites due to tool limits. However, here is what emerged from the sources accessed:

### Pentecostal / Charismatic Distinctive

Precept Austin contains a pointed critique of certain charismatic practices regarding the work of the Holy Spirit, using Ezekiel 2:1-2 as a proof text:

> "It's ironic, when you compare Ezekiel's experience with what happens in a charismatic service today. In a Benny Hinn meeting supposedly it's the Holy Spirit who knocks you down — while it's man who helps you up. But that's not what happens to Ezekiel. The Spirit doesn't knock him down, but helps him up. Ezekiel humbles himself and falls on his face, then the Spirit lifts him up! Guys, don't be mistaken, the Holy Spirit doesn't slay us — He stands us up again, after we've humbled ourselves."

This reflects a cessationist or non-charismatic critique of "slaying in the Spirit" practices, arguing that the biblical pattern is self-humbling followed by the Spirit's empowering to stand and serve, not the Spirit knocking people down.

— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_21-10

### Reformed / Broader Evangelical

The Reformed-leaning sources (JFB, Calvin via PreceptAustin) emphasise God's sovereignty in the call: the divine word is always accompanied by the Spirit, and humiliation is always followed by divine exaltation. Calvin stresses that "God never prostrates his people so as to leave them lying upon the earth, but continually raises them afterwards." The emphasis falls on the inseparability of Word and Spirit — a hallmark of Reformed theology.

— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_21-10

### Baptist (Particular Baptist — Gill)

Gill emphasises Ezekiel as a "type of Christ," noting the prophet's mission to "the rebellious house of Israel" parallels Christ being sent "only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (Matt 15:24). He also stresses the distinction between the Spirit's work and the external word, a point consistent with Puritan and Reformed Baptist theology.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/2.htm

### Methodist / Wesleyan, Lutheran, Anglican, Catholic, Orthodox

I was unable to retrieve material from these traditions' approved sites within the tool limits. Searches directed at lcms.org, 1517.org, wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com, newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org either returned no results or could not be completed.

### Modern Scholarship

I was unable to retrieve the NET Bible notes (netbible.org) or the bibleodyssey.org material within the tool limits. The most scholarly of the sources accessed was Peake's Commentary (via StudyLight, seen in search excerpts), which notes that Ezekiel's inspiration through a written scroll reflects the growing importance of the written word in Israel's religion following the publication of Deuteronomy in 621 BC — a significant departure from Jeremiah's more immediate conception of inspiration via the divine touch on the lips.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-2.html
